name: Nasal strips for sleep

lead: Nasal strips are small adhesive bandages with a flexible plastic spring inside. Stuck across the bridge and sides of the nose, they gently pull the walls of the nostrils outward. People wear them at night to keep the nose open, with the aim of breathing through the nose while asleep, snoring less and waking more rested.

In appearance-focused communities the payoff is framed as a chain: easier nasal breathing leads to better sleep, which is linked by users to a fresher face, less puffiness and less dry mouth, and it supports nasal-breathing habits that some forum members tie to facial development. Controlled studies have repeatedly measured improved nasal airflow with the strips; results for snoring vary between people.

paras: A strip is pressed onto clean, dry skin over the lower part of the nose before bed and peeled off in the morning. Many users pair it with other nasal-breathing practices such as saline rinses or mouth taping. Effects on airflow are felt immediately, so users judge them the first night.

The most commonly reported issue is skin irritation or redness from the adhesive. Reviews find that the strips improve nasal airflow but have not changed measured sleep apnea severity, so they are not a treatment for sleep apnea. People with persistent obstruction or heavy snoring are generally advised by clinicians to have it evaluated.

angle.text: The strip widens the nasal valve while worn, which makes breathing through the nose easier during sleep. Users connect better sleep and nasal breathing with a more rested appearance and less dry mouth; the strip itself does not change the shape of the nose.

lead: Nasal strips for sleep are external nasal dilators, best known under the Breathe Right brand, worn across the nose overnight. A strip is an adhesive band with an elastic plastic spine; as the spine tries to flatten, it lifts the sides of the nose and widens the nasal valve, the narrowest part of the airway.[1][2] The product was cleared by the FDA as a medical device in October 1993 and rose to fame when NFL players wore it on the field in 1994 and 1995.[3]

People use them to look and feel better through a chain: a more open nose supports nasal breathing during sleep, which users link to less snoring, fewer wake-ups, less dry mouth and a fresher face in the morning. Within looksmaxxing circles the strips are discussed alongside mouth taping and myofunctional habits as a low-cost, reversible way to encourage nasal breathing, which some members tie to jaw and midface development.

Research on nasal dilators is extensive. Reviews report that the devices dilate the nasal valve, reduce nasal resistance and improve airflow, with large variation between individuals.[1] A systematic review and meta-analysis found no significant change in apnea-hypopnea index or snoring index in people with obstructive sleep apnea, although nasal breathing itself improved.[4] A 2026 scoping review described the devices as an accessible way of relieving nasal obstruction, with internal dilators showing greater relief than external strips.[5]

The strips sit beside a wider social-media wave around nighttime nasal breathing. A 2025 systematic review in PLOS One was prompted by social media posts promoting mouth taping for better sleep, less dry mouth and anti-aging, and it reported that four of ten included studies flagged asphyxiation risk for people with blocked nasal airways.[6][7] Nasal strips are a different, non-occlusive product that keeps the mouth free.

paras: A nasal strip is a thin adhesive bandage with embedded plastic ribs or splints. It is applied over the bridge and sides of the nose and keeps the sides from collapsing inward during inhalation [2]. During breathing in, negative pressure tends to narrow the nasal valve; the strip stabilises it, and reviews note that airflow improves most on inspiration [1].

Strips come in different sizes and strengths and in clear or skin-toned versions. A separate category, internal dilators such as Nozovent, sits inside the nostrils; reviews often study the two types together [1][4].

The strip was conceived by mechanical designer Bruce Johnson, who formed Creative Integration and Design in 1988, spent about three years developing a spring-loaded adhesive dilator and applied for a patent in 1990.[3] Johnson met Dr. Daniel Cohen, co-founder of Minneapolis company CNS, in October 1991, and CNS licensed the device in February 1992 and funded testing and clinical trials.[3]

The FDA allowed marketing as a medical device in October 1993, cleared the snoring claim in 1995 and, in 1996, added claims for nasal congestion and breathing difficulty from a deviated septum.[3] Early sales were concentrated in the Twin Cities, with drugstore shelf space following in early 1994. In October 1994 Cohen sent strips to NFL trainers; Herschel Walker and Jerry Rice were among the players who wore them, fourth-quarter sales doubled, and about eight Super Bowl XXIX players wore the strip in January 1995.[3]

Annual sales rose from about 2.8 million US dollars in 1994 to 48.5 million in 1995 and 85.9 million in 1996, and CNS agreed in August 1995 that 3M would distribute the product internationally.[3] Exercise studies from the mid-1990s onward examined whether the strips changed performance or oxygen use; Wikipedia summarises these as generally finding no performance-enhancing effect, though wearers reported easier breathing.[2] A veterinary version for horses, licensed to CNS in 1997 by its inventors, was first used publicly at the 1999 Breeders' Cup.[2]

In appearance communities the strips appear mainly in nasal-breathing routines. Users describe wearing them to sleep with the mouth closed, sometimes with mouth tape, with the aim of waking with less dry mouth and fewer signs of poor sleep such as puffiness or tired eyes. Some members also connect habitual nasal breathing with jaw and midface development, a claim discussed in separate entries on nasal breathing and mewing.
Others use them for exercise or for temporary relief of a blocked nose, for example during a cold, which is consistent with the way they are marketed.

The strips are most often cited by people building a night-time routine: saline rinses before bed, a strip across the nose, side or back sleeping, and in some cases mouth taping. Communities that promote nasal breathing present the strip as the least restrictive of these steps, since it does not close the mouth. Nasal breathing is in turn linked by advocates to the tongue-posture and facial-development claims discussed under mewing, a link no published study has tested for strips.

The device lifts the lateral nasal walls. Studies in healthy volunteers report reduced congestive symptoms and increased airflow through the front of the nose [8][2]. Researchers also use the strips diagnostically: surgeons have applied them in assessments to see whether nasal valve obstruction contributes to a patient's breathing difficulty.

Randomised and crossover studies have examined external dilators in snorers, people with chronic rhinitis, patients with sleep-disordered breathing and healthy people. In a randomised placebo-controlled study of twelve non-obese chronic rhinitis patients, polysomnography was used to assess the effect on snoring [9]. A crossover study of eighteen heavy snorers evaluated effects on nasal airway dimensions, sleep architecture and snoring [10]. A study of 26 patients with sleep-disordered breathing measured respiratory disturbance index with and without the strips [11]. Two randomised controlled trials, published in 2019, examined sleep quality and congestion with Breathe Right strips [12].

A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of fourteen studies found nasal dilators improved nasal breathing but produced no significant change in apnea-hypopnea index, lowest oxygen saturation or snoring index in patients with obstructive sleep apnea; internal dilators showed a small reduction in apnea index [4]. A 2006 review concluded the response varies greatly between individuals and that the strips can reduce snoring in selected patients [1]. In children, an external stent increased nasal inspiratory flow in a randomised study [13]. A study of exercise found that the strips delay the switch to mouth breathing, with small effects on performance [1].

Press coverage of the strips has run in two phases: the 1990s sports and snoring marketing wave, and the 2020s wellness wave in which nasal breathing, mouth taping and sleep tracking trend on social media. The 2025 review was explicitly framed as a response to those posts, and its authors described mouth taping as often celebrity-endorsed.[6][7]

Related practices include internal dilators such as Nozovent, which a meta-analysis found gave a small reduction in apnea index in sleep apnea patients; saline irrigation; nasal steroid sprays prescribed for rhinitis; and surgical treatment of nasal valve collapse. Surgeons have also used the strips diagnostically to see whether valve collapse contributes to obstruction.[4]

The most commonly mentioned problem is skin irritation from the adhesive [2]. Clinicians note that heavy snoring or persistent obstruction can have causes such as sleep apnea or a deviated septum that a strip does not address, and reviews emphasise the strips have not shown improvement in sleep apnea outcomes [4][5]. Nasal strips are also used by pregnant patients with rhinitis as a drug-free option for subjective relief [14].

A 2025 PLOS One systematic review of mouth taping, which did not examine nasal strips, reported that four of its ten included studies discussed risks such as asphyxiation when nasal obstruction is present and aspiration from regurgitation; its authors concluded that existing evidence does not support mouth taping as a treatment for sleep-disordered breathing.[6][7] Researcher Brian Rotenberg was quoted in the release saying many people are not appropriate for mouth taping.[7] The distinction matters for strips, which leave the mouth open, but clinicians in these reviews recommend evaluation of persistent obstruction in either case.[4][6]
